title: A Galaxy's Overbright Heart
question: What makes the center of some galaxies shine more than their stars can explain?
hook: At the heart of some galaxies sits an engine that no collection of stars can run.
idea: Matter falling onto a supermassive black hole is theorized to power the extra glow of an active galaxy.

beats.prompt: Telescopes find a galaxy center shining in radio, X-ray and gamma ray light, with far more energy than its starlight explains. What is the likeliest source?

choices.label: An unusually crowded patch of stars
choices.feedback: Tempting because stars do shine, but the radiation from an active nucleus is not produced by stars.

choices.label: Matter accreting onto a supermassive black hole
A dust cloud producing its own light
choices.feedback: Dust can obscure a nucleus's radiation, but it only re-radiates it at another waveband and does not create it.

beats.explain: The non-stellar radiation of an active nucleus is theorized to result from accretion of matter onto a supermassive black hole.

beats.prompt: Put these AGN milestones in the order they were published.
items: Fath detects emission lines from the nuclei of NGC 1068 and Messier 81
Curtis finds the jet in Messier 87
Seyfert describes nearby galaxies with bright nuclei and broad emission lines
Schmidt measures the redshift of the quasar 3C 273

beats.prompt: Match each astronomer to what they did.
pairs: Described nearby galaxies with bright nuclei and unusually broad emission lines
Measured the redshift of the quasar 3C 273
Introduced the concept of active galactic nuclei
Proposed that nearby galaxies hold black holes as relics of dead quasars
beats.explain: Each of them moved forward the idea of what powers an active nucleus.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: A galaxy's center gives off more energy than its stars could produce.
Its light spans radio waves through gamma rays.
Light across so many wavebands must be coming from stars.
So a black hole is not needed to explain it.
beats.explain: The excess emission of an active nucleus is non-stellar: its luminosity is not produced by the stars.
